section.title: Combining functions
section.p: Transformations moved a graph without changing its basic identity. A parabola could shift, stretch, or reflect and still be built from the same old rule.

There is another way to make new functions. We can combine outputs. We can multiply two changing quantities. We can divide one quantity by another. Most importantly, we can feed the output of one function into the input of another.
These operations are not bookkeeping. Later, each one will force a derivative rule.

note.title: Moral
note.p: Simplifying a formula can hide a missing input. A function is not only a formula; it is a formula together with its allowed inputs.

paragraphs.p: This small warning will return when we study limits. Sometimes a function has a hole at one point, but its nearby values still point clearly toward a missing height.

exercise.title: Why can simplifying a formula hide a missing input?

statement.p: The quotient \frac{x^2-1}{x-1} simplifies to x+1 for x\neq1, but it is not the same function as p(x)=x+1 on all real numbers. In your own words, what information does cancellation throw away, and why is a function a formula together with its allowed inputs?

hint.p: Algebra can rewrite values where both formulas are defined. It cannot restore an input that the original expression never allowed.

subsection.title: Composition
subsection.p: Addition, multiplication, and division combine outputs that come from the same input. Composition is different. In composition, the output of one function becomes the input of another.

subsection.title: When an inverse exists
subsection.p: Not every function can be undone.
The problem is duplication. If two different inputs give the same output, then the output does not remember which input produced it.
The square function on all real numbers is the first example:
It sends both 2 and -2 to 4:
An inverse would have to answer the question:
Should the answer be 2 or -2? A function is allowed only one output for each input, so there is no inverse function for x^2 on all of \mathbb R.

statement.p: A function f is one-to-one if different inputs always give different outputs.

note.title: Inverse criterion
note.p: A function has an inverse function exactly when it is one-to-one.

paragraphs.title: The horizontal line test
paragraphs.p: A graph represents a one-to-one function exactly when every horizontal line crosses the graph at most once.
A horizontal line represents one output value. If it hits the graph twice, then two different inputs produced the same output. That prevents an inverse.

Composition and inverses will matter throughout calculus. The chain rule will describe how a composition changes. The derivative of an inverse function will describe how undoing a function changes rates.

But before calculus can use functions well, we need to know the families that appear most often. A formula is more than symbols: it has a shape, a natural domain, a growth pattern, and often a physical meaning.
